week-1.html.title: Week 1
week-1.html.description:
By the end of this lecture you should be able to: Solve simple problems of reflection and refraction Find the critical angle between two media Classify images as being either 'virtual' or 'real' You have likely come across two representation models of light in your previous studies; the particle theory (photons) and the wave theory (electromagnetic waves).While the wave theory of light is great at explaining how light propagates, the particle theory explains many aspects of emission and absorption.We often use the concept of a wave front to describe wave propagation.Definition: Wave Front The locus of all adjacent points at which the phase of vibration of a physical quantity associated with the wave is the same. Wave fronts are inconvenient to visualise in this manner (previous slide), mainly because we are including too much information. Instead, we usually describe wave propagation in terms of rays.Definition: Ray A ray is an imaginary line along the direction of travel of the wave, perpendicular to the wave front.
Light rays are also convenient when representing the particle theory of light, as the ray describes the path of the particles.Geometrical optics is the study of how light rays form images. Before we can understand what is meant by the term ‘image’ we must first learn the rules and laws of ray optics…In Optics I & II, light obeys the following rules: Light is made of rays Rays follow the rules of Euclid’s geometry Rays are received by our eyes Rays travel in a straight line through a uniform medium Change their direction when they meet the surface of a different medium or if the medium is non-uniform Additional considerations for solving problems using geometrical optics: Rays of a given wave are perpendicular to the wave fronts Wavelengths () are much smaller () than the dimension () of apertures, lenses or opaque objects Being able to draw consistent, accurate diagrams is something you will be assessed on.Essential tools A ruler A protractor A pair of compasses RaysSolid line with an arrow halfway along to show the direction of travel
MirrorsSolid line segment without an arrow, often thicker
Normal lines, tangentsDash-dotted line segment drawn with a ruler
Optical axes, construction linesDashed line segment drawn with a ruler
AnglesArc drawn freehand or using a compass centred at the intersection. Measured in radians only ().
PointsSmall cross mark drawn freehand with a label

The law of reflection Upon reflecting on a smooth surface, the angle that the reflected ray makes with the normal to the surface equals the angle that the incident ray makes with the same normal.
An incident ray strikes a flat mirror at a angle relative to the mirror’s surface.3. The law of refraction When a light ray crosses an interface between two media with refraction indices and , the ratio of these indices equals the ratio of the sine of their respective angles with the normal to that interface: What does this mean visually?
Note: The law does not need to specify which ray is incident and which is refracted. It holds in all mathematically allowed cases A light ray goes from the air into water. The angle the incident ray makes with the normal to the interface is . Find the angle made by the refracted ray with the same normal given that the refractive index of water is and that of air is .Answer: From the text , and .The law of refraction:4. Total internal reflection When a light ray reaches an interface from a medium with refraction index larger than that of the new medium , there is a critical angle beyond which total reflection occurs instead of refraction.
5. Fermat’s principle Light travels between two points along the path that takes the least amount of travel time. Example: In a single medium with refractive index :We know that . The colours of light Light comes in different colours, the nature of which can be unravelled by dispersing white light from a glass prism. The index of refraction depends on colour. The index of refraction usually takes the form of Cauchy’s equation: where and are emprical constants.7. The image of an object Given a point object, its image generated by an optical instrument is the locus, if it exists, at which the rays emitted by the object intersect The image is said to be virtual if the rays diverge from it The image is said to be real if the rays converge to it
Short exerciseIs the image produced by a flat mirror virtual or real?Answer:We see that the rays exiting the mirror appear to diverge from the point image. by definition this is a virtual image

info_showOrphanNodes.description: Show nodes that are not connected to any other nodes.

info_showAttachments.description: Show attachments like images and PDFs as nodes in the graph.

info_allowGlobalGraph.description: Allow the user to view the global graph of all nodes.

info_allowExpand.description: Allow the user to pop-out the graph view to take up the whole screen

info_attractionForce.description: How much should linked nodes attract each other? This will make the graph appear more clustered.

info_linkLength.description: How long should the links between nodes be? The shorter the links the more connected nodes will cluster together.

info_repulsionForce.description: How much should nodes repel each other? This will make disconnected parts more spread out.

info_centralForce.description: How much should nodes be attracted to the center? This will make the graph appear more dense and circular.

info_edgePruning.description: Edges with a length above this threshold will not be rendered, however they will still contribute to the simulation. This can help large tangled graphs look more organised. Hovering over a node will still display these links.

info_minNodeRadius.description: How small should the smallest nodes be? The smaller a node is the less it will attract other nodes.

info_maxNodeRadius.description: How large should the largest nodes be? Nodes are sized by how many links they have. The larger a node is the more it will attract other nodes. This can be used to create a good grouping around the most important nodes.
